planting.note: Plant bulbs 'in the green' or dry in early fall, 3-4 inches deep, into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs.

directions: Native to Balkan and Turkish woodlands, this snowdrop is distinguished from the more common Galanthus elwesii and G. nivalis by its narrow, strongly twisted or coiled glaucous leaves that spiral during emergence. Honey-scented white flowers with green-marked inner segments nod above the foliage in late winter to early spring, opening before most deciduous canopy leafs out. Plant among shrubs or at the base of trees where it can colonize undisturbed leaf litter, and allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally before mowing or tidying nearby ground. Established clumps benefit from occasional division immediately after flowering to maintain vigor and encourage spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into gritty, humus-rich, continuously moist but sharply drained soil in a cool, lightly shaded site; protect from hot afternoon sun.

directions: This diminutive alpine from high meadows and moist rocky ledges of the Alps and Carpathians produces tight rosettes of small, rounded, leathery leaves topped in earliest spring by solitary, fringed lilac-blue bells nodding on thread-thin stems, often emerging through the edge of melting snowbanks. It is among the smallest of the snowbells and demands year-round moisture with sharp drainage, thriving in a trough, raised scree bed, or the cool shaded side of a rock garden rather than open sun. Summer heat and drying winds are its chief enemies, so a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, or dappled light beneath open shrubs, suits it best. Divide congested rosettes carefully just after flowering, since the fine roots resent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in cool part shade; a Pyrenean endemic that benefits from shelter from intense midday sun.

directions: Endemic to the western Pyrenees, this snowbell is readily told apart from its Alpine relatives by the conspicuous fine hairs covering its flower stalks and calyces, a feature reflected in its species name. Fringed, bell-shaped flowers in lilac to violet-blue open in spring above rounded, slightly leathery basal leaves, favoring humid rock crevices and streamside ledges in its native range. In cultivation it wants the same cool, evenly moist, gritty root run as other Soldanella species, sited where afternoon shade shields it from scorching sun, such as a north-facing scree or the shaded margin of a woodland rock garden. Keep it free of competing vegetation and divide only sparingly, as recovery from root disturbance is slow.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade along stream banks or damp woodland ground.

directions: Native to damp woodlands and streamside banks across Japan, this low, mat-forming groundcover carries small, rounded, scalloped leaves on creeping stems that root as they spread, forming a dense carpet in constantly moist shade. In early spring it produces tiny clusters of yellow-green, petal-less flowers surrounded by leafy bracts, adding subtle color to the shaded garden floor well before most perennials emerge. It thrives at the edge of a pond, stream, or rain garden where soil never dries out, and spreads readily by rooting stems rather than seed in cultivated settings. Thin or lift unwanted runners in spring to keep it within bounds among smaller companion plants.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently damp, humus-rich soil in deep to partial shade near a water feature or in a bog garden.

directions: Found in wet woodland seeps and stream margins across Japan, Korea, and China, this creeping groundcover is covered in fine soft hairs on its stems and leaves, giving the foliage a slightly felted texture compared to smoother Chrysosplenium relatives. Loose heads of tiny yellow flowers open in early to mid spring amid rounded, toothed leaves, forming a low, spreading mat that thrives where soil remains saturated for much of the year. Use it as a textural groundcover at the damp margin of a shaded pond or rain garden, where its creeping stems knit together into a continuous low carpet. It does not tolerate drying out, so site it only where consistent moisture is guaranteed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade, mimicking the moist montane meadows and open forest of the northern Rockies.

directions: Treated by some botanists as a distinct species and by others as a variety of the more widespread Erythronium grandiflorum, the Idaho fawn lily is native to moist meadow edges and open conifer woods of Idaho and adjacent Washington and Montana, where snowmelt keeps the soil saturated through its brief spring growth period. It bears one or two nodding, clear yellow flowers with reflexed petals above a pair of plain, unmottled green leaves, blooming as snow retreats at mid to high elevation. Grow it in cool, humus-rich soil under open deciduous shade that gets good spring light before tree canopy fills in, then allow it to dry out somewhat during summer dormancy. Because wild populations are limited and slow-growing from seed, source only nursery-propagated bulbs from a reputable native plant or alpine specialist.
